alt.en: People cycling to work along a separate cycle lane beside a road with cars and trees.
alt.es: Gente yendo al trabajo en bici por un carril bici separado, junto a una carretera con coches y árboles.

questions.prompt: Tell me what you see in the two pictures, and how they are similar or different.

segments.text: Both pictures show people on their way to work, but in very different ways.

In the first one, commuters are standing close together on a crowded bus, holding the rails, and one of them is looking at a phone. In the second, people are cycling along a cycle lane that's separate from the road, with cars and trees next to it.
The people on the bus might be tired or fed up, while the cyclists probably feel more relaxed.
What strikes me is that both pictures are about the journey to work, yet the experiences look worlds apart.
On the bus, commuters are packed in, hanging onto the rails, with one glued to a phone, whereas the cyclists have a lane all to themselves, kept apart from the cars, with trees along the road.
By contrast, the passengers could well be exhausted or irritable, while the cyclists are far more likely to be enjoying some fresh air and exercise.

questions.prompt: Which way of getting to work would you prefer, and why?

segments.text: I'd prefer to cycle to work, I think.
It's cheaper than the bus, and I'd get some exercise on the way. The cycle lane in the picture looks safe because it's separate from the cars.
Last summer I cycled to work for a month, and I felt much more awake when I arrived at the office.
The only problem is the weather, but I'd still rather be outside than squashed on a crowded bus.
If I had the choice, I'd go for the cycle lane without a second thought.
What appeals to me most is having control over my own time, since a bus is at the mercy of the traffic and, by the look of it, of far too many other passengers.
I suspect that arriving a bit out of breath would still beat arriving stressed and cramped, although I'd probably think twice on a rainy morning.
All things considered, the bike wins.

questions.prompt: How might cities encourage people to leave their cars at home?

segments.text: I think cities could do a lot to help.
First, they could make public transport cheaper and more frequent, so people don't need a car. They could also build more cycle lanes like the one in the picture.
Another idea is to make drivers pay to enter the city centre, like they do in London.
If the alternatives are good, people will leave their cars at home.
It's partly a question of carrots and sticks.

On the one hand, councils could charge drivers to enter the centre and cut parking spaces; on the other, they'd need to make buses cheaper, quicker and reliable enough that nobody feels they're losing out.
I'd imagine that protected cycle lanes would make a big difference too, since many people would cycle if they felt safe.
What really matters is making the car the least convenient option, not just the most expensive one.

alt.en: A small cottage in the countryside with a garden and hills behind it, and a person working in the garden.
alt.es: Una casita en el campo con jardín y colinas detrás, y una persona trabajando en el jardín.

questions.prompt: Tell me what you see in the two pictures, and how the two places are different.

segments.text: Both pictures show places where people live, but they're very different.

The first one is a tall block of flats in a city, with balconies, and a person is watering plants on one of them. The second is a small cottage in the countryside, with a garden and hills behind it, and a person is working in the garden.
The person on the balcony might miss having a proper garden, while the person at the cottage probably enjoys the peace and quiet.
Both pictures are about where people choose to live, but the settings couldn't be more different.
On one side there's a tall block of flats with balconies, where somebody is watering plants, whereas the other shows a small cottage with a garden, hills behind it and a person busy working outside.
I'd say the balcony plants might be that person's way of having a little green space, while the cottage owner could well have far more room, though perhaps fewer shops nearby.
So it's really city density against country space.

questions.prompt: Which of these two places would you prefer to live in, and why?

segments.text: I'd prefer to live in the city, to be honest.
There's always something to do, and everything is close, like shops, work and public transport. It's also easier to meet friends. In the countryside I'd probably need a car for everything.
I've got a friend who lives in a village, and she spends hours driving every week.
I like the idea of a cottage for a holiday, but not for every day.
It's a tough call, but on balance I'd choose the city.
What I value most is convenience: work, friends and decent transport are all on my doorstep, along with cinemas and restaurants, which is hard to match in a village.
That said, I might feel differently in ten years' time, particularly if I had children and wanted a garden for them.
For now, though, I'd happily trade space for convenience.

questions.prompt: Do you think more people will want to live in the countryside in the future?

segments.text: I think more people will want to, yes.
Lots of people can work from home now, so they don't need to live near the office. Cities are also very expensive, and houses in the country are often cheaper.
For example, a family could get a bigger house with a garden for the price of a small flat.
But not everyone will leave, because young people still love city life.
I wouldn't be surprised if that trend continued.
Remote working has loosened the link between where you work and where you live, and rising rents are pushing many people out of the cities.
Provided the internet and transport in rural areas improve, I could see small towns becoming far more attractive than they are now.
That said, cities will always draw young people, so it's more a rebalancing than an exodus.

alt.en: Two hikers with backpacks walking up a mountain path, with snowy peaks behind them.
alt.es: Dos excursionistas con mochilas subiendo por un sendero de montaña, con picos nevados detrás.

questions.prompt: Tell me what you see in the two pictures, and how they are similar or different.

segments.text: Both pictures show people on holiday, but they're doing very different things.

The first picture shows a busy beach in summer, with umbrellas, people sunbathing on towels, the sea and the sun. In the second, two hikers with backpacks are walking up a mountain path, with snowy peaks behind them.
The people on the beach are probably relaxing, while the hikers might be tired but enjoying the views.
One holiday is calm and sociable, the other is much more active.
These pictures show two quite opposite ideas of a holiday.

On one hand there's a busy beach in summer, with umbrellas, sunbathers on towels and the sea stretching out under the sun; on the other, just two hikers with backpacks climbing a path towards snowy peaks.
The beachgoers are presumably there to switch off, whereas the hikers must be after a challenge, and they'd probably need to be quite fit.
By contrast with the crowds on the sand, the mountain looks far quieter.

questions.prompt: Which kind of holiday would you prefer, and why?

segments.text: I'd prefer the mountain holiday.
I like being active, and walking in the mountains is a good way to see beautiful places. The beach looks too crowded for me, and I find it boring to lie in the sun all day.
Last year I did a walking trip in the Pyrenees, and it was one of my best holidays.
I can relax at the beach for a day, but not for a whole week.
I'd go for the mountains, no question.
What I enjoy about a hike is the sense of achievement; you earn the view rather than just lying there, and it's far less crowded than a beach in August.
Mind you, I might well feel differently after a stressful year, when all I'd want is to do nothing under an umbrella.
But if I had to pick one, it'd be the mountains.

questions.prompt: Do you think tourism does more good than harm to popular places?

segments.text: I think it does both, to be honest.
Tourism brings jobs and money to local people, especially in small towns. But it can also damage the environment and make everything more expensive for the people who live there.
For example, a crowded beach can be full of rubbish at the end of the day.
So I think popular places need clear rules to protect themselves, and tourists should respect them.
It's a double-edged sword, really.

Tourism can be a lifeline for local economies, but when numbers get out of hand, residents get priced out and the very thing that attracted visitors starts to wear away, whether that's a mountain path or a beach.
I'd argue that limiting visitor numbers or charging an entrance fee could well protect fragile places without killing the benefits.
It all depends on how well it's managed.

questions.prompt: Tell me what you see in the two pictures, and how they are similar or different.

segments.text: Both pictures are about shopping, but people are doing it in different ways.

In the first one, a person is sitting on a sofa ordering something on a laptop, and there are several delivery boxes by the door. In the second, shoppers with bags are walking along a high street, past shop fronts and a café.
The person at home has probably ordered quite a lot, while the people on the high street might be enjoying a day out.
Both pictures show shopping, though in completely different settings.
One shows someone on a sofa with a laptop and several delivery boxes already waiting by the door, whereas the other has shoppers with bags strolling past shop fronts and a café.
The person at home might be saving time, while the shoppers outside could well be treating it as a social outing, as there's a café on the street.
So it's convenience on one side and atmosphere on the other.

questions.prompt: Which do you prefer, shopping online or going to the shops, and why?

segments.text: I prefer shopping online for most things.
It's quicker, and I can compare prices easily, which saves me money. I don't have to carry heavy bags or wait in a queue, either.
But for clothes I like to go to the shops, because I want to try things on before I buy them.
So I use both, depending on what I need.
On balance, I lean towards online shopping, although it's not that clear-cut.
What I like is the convenience and the range: I can compare prices in minutes, which the high street simply can't match.
Still, I'd say shops are worth keeping for things like clothes or shoes, where you really need to see and try them first.
So it depends on what I'm buying, and how much of a hurry I'm in.

questions.prompt: What do you think will happen to the high street in the future?

segments.text: I think many high streets will have to change.
More people are buying online, so some shops will probably close. But I don't think they'll disappear completely, because people still like going out to meet friends.
Maybe there'll be more cafés, restaurants and places to do activities instead of shops.
So the high street will become more of a social place.
I'd expect high streets to survive, but in a different form.
Shops selling things you can easily order online are likely to struggle, whereas places offering an experience, like cafés, services or workshops, should hold up far better.
It's even conceivable that councils will turn empty shops into homes or community spaces.
What counts is giving people a reason to go there in person.

questions.prompt: Tell me what you see in the two pictures, and how they are similar or different.

segments.text: Both pictures show people enjoying their free time, but in very different ways.

The first picture shows a crowd at an outdoor concert in the evening, facing a lit stage with a band, and some people have their hands up. In the second, a person is reading a book in an armchair beside a lamp and a bookshelf, and there's a cat on the rug.
The people at the concert are probably excited and full of energy, while the reader seems calm and relaxed.
Both pictures are about leisure, yet they couldn't feel more different.

In one, a whole crowd is facing a lit stage at an outdoor concert in the evening, with some people raising their hands, whereas the other shows a single person in an armchair with a book, a lamp, a bookshelf and a cat on the rug.
The concert-goers are presumably after a shared, noisy experience, while the reader might well be winding down after a long day.
Crowd and energy on one side, solitude and calm on the other.

questions.prompt: Would you rather go to a concert or stay at home with a book, and why?

segments.text: It depends on my mood, but I'd probably choose the concert.
I love live music, and the atmosphere is something you can't get at home. Being with a lot of people who are enjoying the same thing makes it special.
I went to a festival last summer, and I still remember singing along with thousands of strangers.
But after a tiring week, a quiet evening with a book sounds great too.
Honestly, I'd say it hinges on how my week has gone.
What I love about a concert is the atmosphere, that feeling of being part of something bigger, which no recording can match.
That said, if I'd had a draining week, I'd far rather curl up with a book and a cup of tea, and I suspect the cat would be good company too.
If I had to choose just one, I'd still go for the live music.

questions.prompt: Why do you think live events are still so popular, when we can watch almost anything at home?

segments.text: I think it's because live events feel more special.
At home you can watch anything, but you're on your own. At a concert you're in the same place as the artists, and you feel the energy of the crowd.
A concert is also something to look forward to, and you can share it with friends.
So I don't think screens will ever replace it completely.
I think it comes down to the experience.
It's not so much the performance itself as being there, sharing the moment with thousands of other people, that screens simply can't reproduce.
Perhaps it's precisely because so much of our lives is online that we value something real and unrepeatable, which might explain why tickets sell out so fast.
In a way, the more digital life becomes, the more we'll crave live events.
